title: Runtime Tooling
description: Validation, env parsing, CLI args, and config loading — where TypeScript meets real-world input.

challenges.title: Why runtime validation matters
challenges.whyMatters: Config loaded from env vars, files, or APIs is untyped at runtime. Type assertions on parsed JSON give you false confidence — the actual value might be completely wrong.
hints: TypeScript types don't exist at runtime — JSON.parse returns any

choices.label: No problem — TypeScript guarantees the shape at runtime
JSON.parse returns any — if the env var is missing or malformed, you get runtime crashes with no helpful error
process.env is typed so this is safe
The cast to Config causes a runtime type check

challenges.title: Manual runtime validation pattern
challenges.whyMatters: Type guards are how you narrow unknown input to a typed shape — the foundation of every config parser and API response validator.
hints: v is Config in the return type tells TypeScript what the true branch means

choices.label: A)  always returns true — accepts anything
B)  checks the actual shape at runtime before asserting the type
D)  wrong parameter type — defeats the purpose

challenges.title: Write a manual config validator
challenges.description:
Write a function `parseConfig(raw: unknown): AppConfig` where:

  interface AppConfig { host: string; port: number; logLevel: 'debug' | 'info' | 'warn' | 'error'; workers?: number }

It should:
- Throw a descriptive Error if host is missing or not a string
- Throw if port is missing or not a number
- Throw if logLevel is not one of the four valid values
- Default workers to 1 if not provided
- Return a valid AppConfig if all checks pass

No external libraries — pure TypeScript.
challenges.whyMatters: This is the pattern behind every config loader you'll write before reaching for a validation library. Understanding it makes you a much better user of Zod/Yup/etc.
hints: Cast raw to Record<string, unknown> after checking typeof raw === 'object'
Check Array.includes after asserting the array type
Use Number.isFinite for safer number checks than typeof

challenges.title: Env var parsing patterns
challenges.description:
What is wrong with this env var parsing?

  const port: number = process.env.PORT

And what is the correct way to parse PORT as a number with a default of 8080?
challenges.whyMatters: process.env always returns string | undefined — never a number. Getting this wrong means your port is '8080' (a string) and address-in-use checks silently fail.
hints: process.env values are always strings — parseInt or Number() is needed

choices.label: It's fine — Node coerces env vars to the annotated type
Type error: string | undefined is not assignable to number. Fix: const port = parseInt(process.env.PORT ?? '8080', 10)
It works at runtime but TypeScript complains for no reason
process.env.PORT returns a number if the value looks like one

challenges.title: Write a typed env loader
challenges.description:
Write a function `getEnv` with this signature:

  function getEnv(key: string, fallback?: string): string

If the env var is set, return it. If not and fallback is provided, return fallback. If neither, throw `Error: "Missing env var: KEY"`.

Then write typed parsers built on top of getEnv:
- `getEnvInt(key: string, fallback?: number): number` — parses as integer, throws if not a valid integer
- `getEnvBool(key: string, fallback?: boolean): boolean` — 'true'/'1' → true, 'false'/'0' → false, throws otherwise
- `getEnvEnum<T extends string>(key: string, values: T[], fallback?: T): T` — validates against allowed values
challenges.whyMatters: This small library is something you'd write or copy into every new software engineering tool — typed env parsing that fails loudly at startup rather than silently at runtime.
hints: getEnvInt: use parseInt(val, 10) and check Number.isNaN
getEnvEnum: check values.includes(val as T) — the type cast is safe because you validate it

challenges.title: CLI argument typing
challenges.description:
Given a CLI tool called with:

  node tool.js --host localhost --port 8080 --verbose

What is the type of `process.argv` and what does it contain at index 0, 1, and 2?
challenges.whyMatters: Understanding process.argv layout is required before using any arg parsing library — and occasionally you'll parse args manually for simple scripts.
hints: process.argv is string[] — first two elements are node and the script path

choices.label: Record<string, string> — already parsed as key/value

challenges.title: Write a minimal CLI arg parser
challenges.description:
Write a function `parseArgs(argv: string[]): Record<string, string | boolean>` that parses a simple CLI arg format:

- `--key value` → `{ key: 'value' }`
- `--flag` (no value after, or next is another --key) → `{ flag: true }`
- Ignore argv[0] and argv[1] (node + script path)

Example:
  parseArgs(['node', 'script.js', '--host', 'localhost', '--port', '8080', '--verbose'])
  // → { host: 'localhost', port: '8080', verbose: true }
challenges.whyMatters: You'll write or read exactly this function when building deployment scripts, runbooks, and internal CLI tools that don't need a full framework.
hints: Iterate with a for loop, check if current starts with '--'
Peek at next element: if it exists and doesn't start with '--', it's the value; otherwise it's a boolean flag
